usage: country name + 문화, no particle between them — it reads as one compound noun
문화 + 차이; this is the standard phrase for the gap between two cultures, e.g. 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference)
문화 + 를 + 경험하다; 경험하다 (to experience firsthand) is the habitual partner verb, stronger than just 보다
전통 + 문화; often written as one word 전통문화, contrasted with 대중문화 (pop culture)
examples: 저는 한국 문화를 좋아해요.
I like Korean culture.
Simplest frame: 문화 as a plain object with 를. Notice 한국 문화 sits together with no particle inside it.
나라마다 문화가 조금씩 달라요.
Culture differs a little from country to country.
나라마다 = 'every country / from country to country'; 문화가 달라요 is the everyday way to say cultures differ — 다르다, not 틀리다.
외국에서 살면 처음에는 문화 차이 때문에 힘들 수 있어요.
When you live abroad, at first it can be hard because of cultural differences.
Real-situation register: 문화 차이 때문에 (because of cultural difference) is the exact phrase Koreans reach for to explain culture shock politely.
nuance: 문화 means 'culture' in the broad sense — the customs, arts, food, and shared ways of life of a group. It is Sino-Korean, 文化 ('writing/civilization' 文 + 'become/transform' 化), literally 'becoming civilized', so it leans toward the refined, collective sense of culture rather than one person's habits. The nearest trap-word is 문학 文學 (literature): the two look and sound almost identical, but 학 'study' vs 화 'transform' completely changes the meaning, so an English speaker who half-hears the word can easily swap them. 문화 also is NOT used for bacterial 'culture' (that is 배양) or for being a 'cultured/refined person' (that is 교양 있다). It loves to form compounds — 대중문화 (pop culture), 문화재 (cultural heritage), 문화생활 (cultural life/leisure) — and the habitual verb is 경험하다 (to experience), as in 다른 문화를 경험하다. The everyday phrase 문화 차이 (cultural difference) is how Koreans tactfully explain awkward moments. Register is neutral, fine in both casual chat and formal writing.

mistakes: Confusing 문화 (culture, 文化) with 문학 (literature, 文學). They differ by one syllable (화 vs 학); saying 한국 문학에 관심이 있어요 means 'interested in Korean literature', not culture. Listen for 화 'transform' vs 학 'study'.
Using 틀리다 to say cultures 'are different': 나라마다 문화가 틀려요 literally means each culture is 'wrong'. The correct verb is 다르다 → 문화가 달라요. 틀리다 = incorrect; 다르다 = different.
Adding a particle inside the compound: writing 한국의 문화 sounds stiff and over-literal in speech. Natural spoken Korean drops it — 한국 문화 — treating the two nouns as one unit.

usage: 감동 + 을 받다; the standard way to say YOU were moved — literally 'to receive emotion'. This is the most common form.
감동 + 을 주다; literally 'to give emotion' — used when a film, person, or story moves others
감동 + 적이다 makes the adjective; modifier form 감동적인 영화 (a moving film)
casual/slang; 감동 먹었어 = 'I was so touched' among friends — never in formal writing
examples: 그 영화 정말 감동이었어요.
That movie was really moving.
Simplest frame: 감동이다 used directly as 'was moving'. Casual-polite 요-speech, the most natural quick reaction.
할머니 편지를 읽고 감동을 받았어요.
I read grandma's letter and was moved.
Everyday frame: 감동을 받다 = the experiencer was touched. Note 을 받다 ('receive'), not 했다 — this is how Korean frames being moved.
선수의 마지막 인사가 모든 사람에게 큰 감동을 줬어요.
The athlete's final farewell gave everyone deep emotion.
Real-situation: 감동을 주다 (give emotion) flips the viewpoint to the SOURCE. 큰 감동 (great emotion) is the natural collocation, not 많은 감동.
nuance: 감동 is the warm, welling-up feeling of being moved or touched — the lump-in-the-throat reaction to a kind gesture, a film, or a reunion. It is Sino-Korean, 感動 ('feel' 感 + 'move/stir' 動), literally 'the heart being moved', which is exactly the English metaphor 'to be moved', so the image transfers nicely. The key learner difficulty is the verb frames: Korean splits 'being moved' (감동을 받다, 'receive emotion') from 'moving others' (감동을 주다, 'give emotion'), and the standalone verb 감동하다/감동받다 means YOU felt it — never 'to move a physical object' (that is 옮기다 or 움직이다). Compare the near-synonym 인상 印象 (impression): 인상 깊다 ('it left a deep impression') is more neutral and cognitive, while 감동 is purely emotional and positive. Compare also 감격 (overwhelming emotion, often tears) which is stronger and rarer. Natural collocations: 감동을 받다/주다, 큰 감동 (not 많은 감동), 감동적인 N. Tone is sincere and a touch earnest; the slang 감동 먹다 is friendly but casual only.

Saying 많은 감동 for 'a lot of emotion'. Korean counts this feeling by size, not amount, so the natural phrase is 큰 감동 (great/deep emotion). 많은 감동 sounds off.
Mixing up who feels it: using 감동을 줬어요 when you mean YOU were touched. 주다 = give (you moved others); to say you yourself were moved, use 감동을 받았어요 or 감동했어요.

usage: 하다 verb → drop 하다, the 여 fuses to 해, giving 다양해요 (polite present). The 요-form anchor for this word.
modifier form 다양한 + noun; 다양한 종류, 다양한 의견 are common partners
종류가 + 다양하다; the thing that varies takes 가/이 — 색깔이 다양하다, 의견이 다양하다
adverb form 다양하게; 다양하게 즐기다 (enjoy in various ways), 다양하게 준비하다
examples: 메뉴가 다양해요.
The menu is diverse.
Simplest frame: [N]이/가 다양해요. As a 하다-adjective, 다양 + 해요; the subject (what varies) takes 가.
사람마다 생각이 다양해서 재미있어요.
Everyone thinks differently, so it's interesting.
Everyday frame with 다양해서 (because it's varied). Shows the 해서 reason form and the collocation 생각이 다양하다.
이번 축제에서는 다양한 나라의 음식을 맛볼 수 있어요.
At this festival you can taste food from various countries.
Real-situation: 다양한 + N as a modifier in a full sentence. 다양한 나라의 음식 = 'food from many different countries' — note the variety nuance, not mere counting.
nuance: 다양하다 means 'to be various / diverse', stressing a wide RANGE of different kinds, not just a big number. It is a 하다-adjective from Sino-Korean 多樣 ('many' 多 + 'shape/kind' 樣), literally 'many shapes', which captures its core sense of qualitative variety. Because it is a descriptive adjective, the present polite form follows 하다-conjugation — 다양 + 해요 — and the noun-modifying form is 다양한 N (never 다양하는 N, the present-participle ending reserved for action verbs). The near-synonym trap is 여러 (several) and the number-word 많다 (to be many): 여러 나라 and 많은 나라 simply count 'several / many countries', while 다양한 나라 highlights that they are DIFFERENT in kind. So '메뉴가 많아요' = there are lots of menu items; '메뉴가 다양해요' = the items are varied in type — a real distinction English 'a variety of' blurs. The thing that varies takes 이/가 (종류가 다양하다, 의견이 다양하다), and the adverb 다양하게 pairs with verbs (다양하게 준비하다). Register is neutral, equally at home in casual speech and formal writing.

mistakes: Using the verb-style modifier 다양하는 N. 다양하다 is an adjective, so the modifier is 다양한 (다양한 메뉴). 다양하는 is ungrammatical here because -는 marks ongoing action verbs, not descriptive adjectives.
Swapping 다양하다 for 많다 when you mean 'many'. 친구가 다양해요 sounds odd (your friends are 'of varied types'); to say you have many friends use 친구가 많아요. Reserve 다양하다 for difference in kind.
Marking the varied thing with 을/를: 메뉴를 다양해요 is wrong. Adjectives take a subject, not an object — the varying thing gets 이/가: 메뉴가 다양해요.
